title: Other religions (Nostra Aetate, 1965)
hookLine: the Church rejects nothing true and holy in other religions

cards: Athens, the first century. Paul walks through the city and sees altars everywhere, one with an inscription: to the unknown god.
Invited to speak on the Areopagus, a hill where the city's thinkers gathered, he doesn't mock their altars. He starts from one of them and reaches for words they already know.
"For in him we live, and move, and are," he says, and adds that some of their poets had said we are God's offspring.
Nineteen centuries later, the Catholic Church wrote a short document about people of other religions, and it sounds a lot like Paul on that hill.

teach.b: In 1965 the Second Vatican Council issued a declaration named by its first Latin words: Nostra Aetate, in our age.
Its central sentence: the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions.
It speaks with sincere respect of their ways of living and acting and their teachings, which, it says, often reflect a ray of the truth that enlightens all people.
It names Hindus and Buddhists and their searching, and speaks with esteem of Muslims, who worship the one God and honor Abraham, Jesus as a prophet, and Mary.

The same document says the Church also keeps proclaiming Christ, and holds both together. A whole section is about the Jewish people. It speaks of the great spiritual heritage Christians share with them.

teach.h: NO COLLECTIVE BLAME ON THE JEWS.
teach.b: It says that what happened in Christ's passion cannot be charged against all the Jews of that time, or against Jews today. And it deplores hatred and antisemitism at any time and from any source.
After centuries of that charge, those sentences were written down at a council.
In 1986, Pope John Paul II invited leaders of many religions to Assisi to pray for peace, each in their own way, side by side.
The Church asks Catholics to meet their neighbors of other faiths with respect, to learn, and to work together for the good.
Nothing true is rejected: not because every belief is the same, but because truth, wherever it's found, is taken seriously.

how: Catholic dioceses run interreligious dialogue offices, parishes share service projects and study with neighboring synagogues, mosques and temples, and popes have met leaders of other religions, as at Assisi in 1986.

o: faiths beyond Christianity, met with respect
ancient faiths that no one practices anymore
beliefs the Church prefers to stay silent about

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: leaders of many faiths pray for peace

s: Nostra Aetate says the Church rejects nothing true and holy in other religions
and it speaks with sincere respect of their ways of life and teaching.
Nostra Aetate blames all Jews for the death of Christ
it says the passion can't be charged against all Jews then or today, and deplores antisemitism.
Paul began his speech in Athens by mocking the altars
he began from their altar to the unknown god, and went on to quote their own poets.

games.q: you're Paul in Athens, surrounded by altars to many gods, one marked to the unknown god. how do you begin?
o: by starting from their own altar, and their own poets.
games.why: Paul starts from what they already know: the unknown god, and their poets' line that we are God's offspring.

practice: Here is a prayer Jews say every morning and evening, from Deuteronomy, to hear as a guest, not to pray as your own: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one."

Let it sound in you slowly, and think of the people who will say it tonight before they sleep. If you know someone of another faith, think of them too, and of the words they pray, and hold them with respect.

wordCard.voice: Other religions. How the Catholic Church, since Nostra Aetate in 1965, speaks of other faiths: with respect, rejecting nothing true and holy in them. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: in our age, the first words and name of the 1965 declaration.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing true is rejected. Paul started from their altar. That's day three hundred twenty-one.
